newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin doesn't plan French referendum on euro-aide.
newsitem.headline: Jospin doesn't plan French referendum on euro-aide.

text.p: Prime Minister Lionel Jospin will "sound out" the French people if he has to choose between the terms for a single European currency and preserving economic growth but he does not plan a referendum, aides said on Friday.

The Communist party, which has campaigned for a referendum, earlier welcomed a remark in Jospin's first television interview since he took office which it said might mean he would consult the people before joining economic and monetary union (EMU).
But a source close to the prime minister said: "When he spoke of addressing the French people, he was not talking about a referendum but of a more direct contact."
Jospin said on Thursday that if the government had to make a choice between qualifying for the single currency and preserving economic growth, he would put the issue to the country.

"We will try to define a path which takes account of these contradictory factors," Jospin said. "If there has to be a choice in one direction rather than the other, we...will present the issues of this choice to the country and by its reaction, its indications, it will help us decide."
He added: "In any case, it will be our responsibility to take the decisions. But we will do it without hiding anything or manipulating anything, by telling the truth."
Jospin did not spell out how the country would make its preference known and Communist parliamentary floor leader Alain Bocquet said he had given citizens room to have their say.

"I didn't precisely hear the word referendum, but it seems to me absolutely indispensible to consult the French people before the European challenges and choices of tomorrow," Bocquet told Radio Luxembourg.

However, the source close to Jospin said: "There are plenty of ways of sounding out the country -- through its parliamentary representatives, trade unions, notably at the wages conference (planned later this year), other social forces, opinion polls, reactions around us, the media. We don't need to organise something artificial."

The source stressed Jospin was not talking about a choice for or against the euro, but of ways of reconciling the drive for the single currency with the government's other priorities of growth, jobs and social justice.
If difficult choices have to be made, "he will address the French people, he will make them his witnesses".

In this year's parliamentary election campaign Jospin opposed a referendum on the euro, saying the French people had already approved the Maastricht treaty by referendum in September 1992 and France had given its word.
The source said Jospin would use a speech to his Socialist party's national council on Saturday to continue his effort to explain the difficult choices the government is facing.
"We are moving on from the campaign period to the period of confrontation with reality," he said.
